newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs vie for control of army. [CORRECTED 00:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs vie for control of army. [CORRECTED 00:35 GMT]

text.p: Bosnian Serb civilian leaders vied with ousted generals for control of the army as the government tried to force the military under its sway.

President Biljana Plavsic swore in a new commander of the Bosnian Serb Army (BSA) after dismissing General Ratko Mladic and senior commanders who fought beside him in the 1992-95 separatist war with Moslems and Croats.
Mladic, indicted for war crimes by the United Nations and reported to be ailing, kept a low profile but sources at his headquarters claimed he retained the army's loyalty.

They dismissed the newly appointed army commander and his deputy as lightweights, and one source told Reuters: "Not a single BSA officer -- let alone the (dismissed) generals -- have offered them any support.
"The headquarters staff remains in control of the entire BSA. All commanders at all levels are informing us that they recognise only our command."
Mladic, a hero among Bosnian Serbs, survived a similar attempt to sack him last year, but the army has been weakened since peace was restored and influence funnelled to the police.
NATO peacekeepers and international mediators are watching the internal power struggle nervously, hoping it will not derail the precarious peace process in Bosnia.
Plavsic swore in General Pero Colic as the new commander and General Dragan Josipovic as his deputy in an effort to seal civilian control over the post-war army.
Plavsic blamed international pressure for the move but diplomats said it was probably convenient for her to get rid of Mladic, an aggressive commander who political leaders found hard to control.
The headquarters source dismissed Colic as a former colonel pulled out of a retirement, and Josipovic for never having undergone advanced military studies.
Colic riposted that the new commanders were combat tested and told reporters: "The basis of this new general staff is that we proved ourselves on the battlefield -- we're not armchair generals."
Diplomats suspected Serb President Slobodan Milosevic's hand (corrects from "Bosnian Serb President..." to delete word "Bosnian") lay behind the purge for both domestic and foreign policy reasons.
Milosevic, the guarantor of Bosnian Serb compliance with the U.S.-sponsored peace agreement, needs to reassure the West in order to achieve the lifting of the remaining sanctions against Yugoslavia.
But he acted similarly in 1992 when he axed scores of generals after withdrawing the old Yugoslav Federal Army (JNA) from secessionist wars in Croatia and Bosnia.
The JNA leadership, wedded to the continuation of a united, communist Yugoslavia, represented a threat to his strategy of Serb retrenchment within the borders of a Greater Serbia.
Mladic and his general staff, all veterans of the JNA and faithful to its traditions, represented a similar threat to the concept of compromise in Bosnia.
